paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover the centers of overlapping Gaussian distributions from samples of their mixture. Its setting uses equally weighted spherical Gaussians with identity covariance. A central question is how far apart their centers must be for accurate recovery to be computationally and statistically feasible.

The authors develop an algorithm that estimates the mixture’s Fourier transform at carefully selected frequencies. In dimensions up to order log(k)/log log(k), it efficiently learns the centers with separation roughly d/√log(k), allowing doubly logarithmic factors. This improves on the larger separation threshold associated with the previously understood higher-dimensional regime.

The paper also establishes necessity of the stated separation scale, helping nearly identify the threshold for efficient learning when combined with earlier results. More generally, runtime is polynomial in the number of components with additional dependence on dimension, separation, and accuracy. The approach also extends to non-Gaussian mixtures when their Fourier spectra satisfy a stated mild condition.
neurips-2022-a-fourier-approach-to-mixtu.tldr: Carefully chosen Fourier measurements enable efficient Gaussian-mixture learning at smaller separation scales in low dimensions.

paragraphs: Pathology models often make predictions from images containing many regions, using multiple instance learning to combine the regional information. Inspecting how those regions contribute matters when developers and physicians need to understand a prediction or investigate a failure. This paper introduces Additive MIL, a formulation that builds interpretability into the prediction process.

The central change makes it possible to compute and visualize each image region’s exact contribution to the model’s output. The authors show that existing MIL models can be made additive through a simple change in function composition. This provides a direct accounting of regional contributions while maintaining predictive performance similar to the original models.

The reported spatial contributions align with regions pathologists use during diagnosis and improve on conventional attention heatmaps. The authors also demonstrate applications to debugging failures, detecting spurious features, and identifying regions relevant to individual classes. These findings make the method useful for inspecting model behavior in clinical decision-making contexts, where a prediction alone provides limited insight into its basis.
neurips-2022-additive-mil-intrinsically-.tldr: Additive MIL exposes exact regional contributions to pathology predictions while retaining similar predictive performance.

paragraphs: Bayesian coresets reduce inference cost by replacing a full dataset with a small, weighted subset. Finding useful weights efficiently is difficult, even when accurate coresets appear to exist. Existing approaches can also require a separate inference procedure after constructing the subset and lack bounds on marginal evidence.

Sparse Hamiltonian flows combine the weighted subset with a dynamical inference mechanism. The method starts by uniformly subsampling data, then optimizes a Hamiltonian flow whose parameters include the coreset weights. Periodic momentum quasi-refreshment steps form another part of this flow. Together, these components address construction cost, subsequent inference, and evidence bounds within one method.

The theory establishes exponential dataset compression in a representative model and shows that the quasi-refreshment steps reduce KL divergence to the target distribution. The compression result therefore has a specific model setting. Experiments on real and synthetic data report accurate posterior approximations with substantially lower runtime than competing inference methods based on dynamical systems.
neurips-2022-bayesian-inference-via-spar.tldr: Sparse Hamiltonian flows jointly optimize weighted data subsets and posterior approximations to reduce Bayesian inference cost.

paragraphs: The paper asks how neural circuits might learn the transformations that occur when objects move. It represents images as vectors of pixel intensities and considers translations and rotations through orthogonal transformations. The mathematical framework breaks transformations into smaller rotational components, focusing on commuting transformations, whose order of application does not matter.

The authors propose two learning mechanisms for these irreducible representations. The first uses a singular value decomposition of an anti-symmetrized outer product formed from consecutive images and has a single-layer neural implementation. The second applies principal component analysis to differences between successive frames. It requires two layers but is described as more biologically plausible.

Both networks learn image rotations and translations, with the rotation results reproducing earlier work. The contribution connects a mathematical account of visual transformations to candidate neural learning mechanisms. Its biological claim remains a possibility: the paper proposes looking for these networks in connectivity and physiology data, rather than reporting that the brain has already been shown to implement them.
neurips-2022-biological-learning-of-irre.tldr: Two biologically motivated neural mechanisms learn component representations of commuting image transformations.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input falls outside the data a model is expected to handle. This paper examines the internal features used to make that judgment. Its starting point is typicality: the authors identify a feature’s typical set with a high-probability region of the model’s feature distribution.

Their method rectifies features into these typical sets before computing an out-of-distribution score. This changes the representation supplied to the scoring procedure and is intended to improve uncertainty estimation. The rectification can be attached as a plug-and-play module to different scoring methods, giving it a role across multiple existing detection approaches.

Evaluations cover CIFAR and the higher-resolution ImageNet benchmark with its larger label space. On ImageNet, the paper reports improvements over state-of-the-art methods of up to 5.11% in average FPR95. The stated result supports feature rectification as a useful component of detection on these benchmarks; the maximum improvement should be understood as the reported best extent of the gain.
neurips-2022-boosting-out-of-distributio.tldr: Rectifying internal features into high-probability regions improves out-of-distribution detection with multiple scoring methods.

paragraphs: People refer to objects through combinations of speech and gestures. Learning to interpret these combinations requires data that captures both signals and the viewpoints from which they are observed. Collecting real interactions is costly, while existing synthetic tools often omit gestures and available multimodal datasets may cover only an outside observer’s view.

CAESAR is an embodied simulator designed to generate referring expressions with verbal and nonverbal information from multiple views. The authors use it to create two large-scale datasets, which they report having released publicly. This makes viewpoint and gesture information part of the generated interaction data available for studying how expressions connect to objects and spatial relationships.

Experiments evaluate spatial relation grounding with several state-of-the-art baseline models. The results suggest that visual perspective affects performance and that nonverbal information improves grounding accuracy. These findings support studying language alongside gesture and viewpoint. The abstract also states an intention to release the simulator so researchers can generate additional embodied interaction datasets.
neurips-2022-caesar-an-embodied-simulato.tldr: CAESAR generates multiview language-and-gesture datasets, with experiments suggesting gestures improve spatial relation grounding.

paragraphs: A learned prediction can give an optimization algorithm a useful starting point, potentially reducing the work needed to reach an optimal solution. Earlier work demonstrated this idea for weighted perfect bipartite matching using predicted dual solutions. This paper develops a broader framework for such warm starts through discrete convex analysis.

Discrete convex analysis supplies a counterpart to convex analysis for discrete optimization problems. The authors apply their framework to weighted perfect bipartite matching, weighted matroid intersection, and discrete energy minimization in computer vision. These applications show how the same mathematical perspective can guide prediction-assisted algorithms across several problem types.

The resulting runtime bounds depend on the largest coordinate error between the predicted and optimal solutions, expressed through the infinity norm. Earlier bounds depended on the sum of coordinate errors through the one norm. The paper establishes smaller time-complexity bounds and more sample-efficient prediction learning with its approach. It also uses this perspective to discuss whether learning primal or dual solutions is preferable.
neurips-2022-discrete-convex-analysis-ba.tldr: Discrete convex analysis yields prediction-based warm starts with improved runtime bounds and more sample-efficient learning.

paragraphs: One-shot generative models create new examples of an unfamiliar visual concept after seeing a single example. Evaluating this ability requires attention to both variation and preservation of the concept’s identity. The paper argues that commonly used generative-model metrics do not adequately support this setting or precise comparisons with human generation.

The authors introduce an evaluation framework with two axes: how recognizable generated samples are and how much they vary within a class. They use it to systematically study representative models on the Omniglot handwriting dataset. GAN-like and VAE-like models occupy opposite ends of the resulting diversity–recognizability space, exposing differences that a single score could obscure.

Analyses of model parameters find linear contributions from spatial attention and context integration to the observed trade-off. Disentanglement instead moves performance along a parabolic curve that could help maximize recognizability. Using these comparisons, the authors identify model configurations that closely approximate human data, providing a more targeted way to study human-like generation in this setting.
neurips-2022-diversity-vs-recognizabilit.tldr: A diversity–recognizability framework reveals how one-shot generative models and their parameters compare with human examples.

paragraphs: The paper studies a platform that must assign arriving jobs to workers while learning which matches are valuable. A job’s type is visible on arrival, but the platform initially lacks knowledge of worker-type frequencies and average rewards for worker–job type combinations. Its objective is to maximize total payoff over a planning horizon.

To model a large market and choice overload, the analysis assumes an unlimited worker supply, with worker attributes drawn from an underlying population distribution. The authors establish lower bounds on regret, measuring the performance cost of learning, and propose an online algorithm that adapts to the unknown distribution and payoffs as matching proceeds.

The algorithm is rate-optimal relative to the established limits. A distinctive theoretical finding is that achievable performance depends only at second order on the worker-type distribution. This identifies a particular way that population composition enters the learning guarantees. The authors suggest that this dependence may have broader relevance, while their demonstrated result concerns the stated sequential matching model.
neurips-2022-dynamic-learning-in-large-m.tldr: A rate-optimal online algorithm learns profitable job–worker matches under unknown worker populations and match payoffs.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization chooses which evaluations of an expensive black-box function to request. Information-based approaches often select queries that reduce uncertainty about the optimum, measured with Shannon entropy. This paper asks how query selection should change when the useful information depends on a particular downstream decision.

The authors adopt a decision-theoretic generalization of entropy parameterized by a task-specific loss function. That loss describes how inferred information will be used, allowing the uncertainty measure to reflect the eventual objective. They show that special cases recover familiar acquisition functions, including knowledge gradient, expected improvement, and entropy search.

Changing the loss produces a flexible family of acquisition functions for other optimization settings. The paper also develops gradient-based methods to optimize these functions efficiently. Experiments report strong performance across sequential decision tasks involving variants of top-k optimization, multi-level set estimation, and sequence search. The contribution thus combines a common interpretation of existing methods with a mechanism for designing query policies around different downstream goals.
neurips-2022-generalizing-bayesian-optim.tldr: Task-specific decision losses generalize entropy-based Bayesian optimization and yield customizable query-selection rules.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why neural networks can change their predictions under small adversarial perturbations. It identifies natural settings in which depth-two ReLU networks trained by gradient flow are provably vulnerable to small changes measured in the Euclidean norm. The result concerns the behavior induced by the training procedure in those settings.

Crucially, robust networks that correctly classify the training data also exist in the settings studied. Vulnerability therefore cannot be explained simply by saying that fitting those data requires a non-robust network. The analysis instead connects the outcome of training to an implicit preference for solutions that maximize the classification margin.

The authors prove that every network satisfying the KKT conditions of the relevant max-margin problem is non-robust under their setting. These conditions connect the margin optimization problem to the networks selected by gradient-based training. The finding shows how a familiar optimization bias can favor adversarial vulnerability even when robust solutions are available, without asserting that every architecture or every training problem behaves this way.
neurips-2022-gradient-methods-provably-c.tldr: In identified settings, gradient flow favors non-robust depth-two ReLU networks even though robust classifiers exist.

paragraphs: A classifier may encounter different data conditions after deployment, making it important to specify what stays stable across domains. Causal relationships offer one possible source of stability. However, a strategy that predicts a label only from its causal parents is unhelpful in the anti-causal setting studied here, where the label causes the observed covariates.

The paper develops representation learning for a particular form of domain shift that preserves shared causal structure while accommodating this anti-causal relationship. It translates the causal assumptions into learning principles that separate invariant features from features that can change across domains. This separation is the central mechanism of the proposed approach.

The learned representation supports both an invariant predictor and fast adaptation to new domains. These are complementary uses of the shared structure: maintaining stable predictive information while retaining information useful for adjustment. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the algorithm’s effectiveness. The result is tied to the specified causal account of domain shift, rather than an unrestricted claim about every deployment mismatch.
neurips-2022-invariant-and-transportable.tldr: Separating stable and changing features under shared causal assumptions supports invariant prediction and fast domain adaptation.

paragraphs: Self-supervised speech models can reduce dependence on transcribed audio, but their growing size creates difficulties for devices with limited resources. Supporting several languages or tasks can intensify this problem. Large models can also overfit when adapted to small speech datasets, making efficient adaptation an accuracy concern as well as a resource concern.

The proposed S³-Router framework adapts model connections. The authors report that discarding no more than 10% of weights through connection fine-tuning can achieve better downstream accuracy than standard weight fine-tuning. This finding suggests that selecting which existing connections remain active can provide an effective route to adapting speech representations.

The framework is presented as serving four purposes: a fine-tuning scheme, an efficient multilingual and multitask solution, a state-of-the-art pruning technique, and a tool for quantitatively analyzing learned representations. Its stated contribution is the combination of improved efficiency and reduced overfitting through connection selection. The reported accuracy advantage supports that approach for the downstream speech tasks examined.
neurips-2022-losses-can-be-blessings-rou.tldr: S³-Router adapts speech-model connections, reporting better accuracy than weight fine-tuning while removing at most 10% of weights.

paragraphs: MILE jointly learns a model of the driving environment and a policy for acting within it. Training uses an offline collection of expert urban-driving demonstrations, without online interaction with the environment. The approach uses three-dimensional geometry to guide learning a compact internal representation directly from high-resolution video.

The learned model can predict multiple plausible future states and actions. Its internal predictions can be decoded into semantic bird’s-eye views, making the imagined scene interpretable. The authors also demonstrate complex driving maneuvers executed from plans generated entirely through these internal predictions, connecting world modeling to the policy’s behavior.

In CARLA, MILE improves driving score by 31% over the prior state of the art when evaluated in a new town and new weather conditions. This provides simulator evidence for generalization beyond the training conditions. The authors also identify their approach as the first camera-only urban-driving method to model the static scene, moving agents, and the vehicle’s own behavior together.
neurips-2022-model-based-imitation-learn.tldr: MILE learns a driving world model and policy from offline video, improving CARLA driving score under new conditions.

paragraphs: The paper studies multiclass classification with a bounded number of labels in the realizable setting. It extends traditional PAC learning in two directions: rates that depend on the data distribution and learning guarantees that incorporate assumptions about the data’s structure. Both directions refine how learnability is described.

For universal learning, the authors characterize achievable rates for every fixed distribution. They establish a three-way classification: a concept class has an optimal rate that is exponential, linear, or arbitrarily slow. They also provide complexity measures of the hypothesis class that determine which of these cases applies, connecting abstract class structure to learning speed.

The second contribution concerns partial concept classes, whose functions may be undefined on some inputs. These can express structured-data settings such as low-dimensional manifolds or margin conditions. The paper extends PAC learnability from total to partial concepts in multiclass classification and investigates differences between them. Together, the results describe learning behavior beyond guarantees that treat distributions and input structure uniformly.
neurips-2022-multiclass-learnability-bey.tldr: The paper characterizes universal multiclass learning rates and extends PAC learnability to partially defined concepts.

paragraphs: Reward-free reinforcement learning studies exploration without using a reward objective to guide the data collection. This paper examines its sample requirements with general nonlinear function approximation. The focus is on which structural assumptions permit efficient exploration and which leave the problem statistically difficult.

The authors introduce RFOLIVE and prove sample-efficient reward-free exploration under structural assumptions broad enough to cover linear Markov decision processes, linear completeness, and low-rank models with unknown representations. Their analysis shows that previously used explorability or reachability assumptions are not statistically necessary in the latter two settings. This removes particular requirements from the sample-efficiency account.

A complementary hardness result concerns linear completeness when the underlying features are unknown. In that case, the authors establish statistical difficulty for both reward-free and reward-aware exploration, yielding an exponential separation from the low-rank setting. Together, the results show that closely related structural descriptions can imply very different data requirements, and that knowing the features matters to how these guarantees should be interpreted.
neurips-2022-on-the-statistical-efficien.tldr: RFOLIVE broadens sample-efficient reward-free exploration, while hardness results separate unknown-feature linear completeness from low-rank models.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks can perform well with few time steps, but commonly used backpropagation through time requires substantial training memory. It also differs from learning rules that update as activity unfolds. This paper introduces online training through time, or OTTT, to support forward-in-time learning while retaining useful optimization behavior.

Derived from backpropagation through time, OTTT tracks presynaptic activity and uses instantaneous losses and gradients. Its memory requirement stays constant with respect to the number of time steps. The authors prove that its gradients provide a similar descent direction to gradients from equivalent spike-representation mappings in both feedforward and recurrent settings.

The update takes the form of three-factor Hebbian learning, creating a possible route toward online learning on neuromorphic hardware. This connects two major supervised training approaches for spiking networks within a biologically plausible formulation. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and CIFAR10-DVS report superior performance with few time steps on static and neuromorphic data; on-chip learning remains a prospective application.
neurips-2022-online-training-through-tim.tldr: OTTT trains spiking networks forward in time with memory independent of sequence length and theoretically supported descent directions.

paragraphs: The paper studies offline learning for linear contextual bandits, where decisions must be learned from existing data. It considers pessimistic learning rules built from confidence sets. These sets represent uncertainty, and their geometry becomes a central design choice in the proposed family of rules.

The family uses different p-norms to define the confidence sets. Its two-norm member corresponds to Bellman-consistent pessimism. Its infinity-norm member provides a new extension of lower-confidence-bound learning to the linear setting. Placing these rules in one family allows the authors to compare their performance through a common mathematical framework.

The main result establishes a qualified form of adaptive optimality for the infinity-norm rule: it achieves minimax performance up to logarithmic factors across all q-norm-constrained problems considered. In this theoretical sense, it strictly dominates the other members of the family, including the two-norm rule. The result shows that the choice of confidence-set geometry can materially affect the strength and adaptability of offline learning guarantees.
neurips-2022-pessimism-for-offline-linea.tldr: An infinity-norm pessimistic rule achieves adaptive minimax guarantees, up to logarithmic factors, across the studied constrained bandit problems.

paragraphs: Feature upsampling increases spatial resolution inside a prediction model. For dense prediction, the resulting features should remain coherent within semantic regions while preserving sharp boundaries between them. This paper introduces point affiliation: the assignment of an upsampled point to a local cluster of decoder features with similar semantic content.

The method constructs upsampling kernels by comparing an encoder feature at a location with nearby decoder features. That comparison supplies a cue about which semantic cluster the new point should belong to. The resulting similarity-aware kernels are designed to encourage both smooth regions and distinct boundaries in the expanded feature map.

The authors implement this formulation as a lightweight operator called SAPA and investigate variants of it. They report consistent improvements across semantic segmentation, object detection, depth estimation, and image matting. These results support the usefulness of semantic affiliation across several dense prediction tasks. The contribution is a general formulation for upsampling kernels together with a practical operator that instantiates it.
neurips-2022-sapa-similarity-aware-point.tldr: SAPA uses encoder–decoder feature similarity to upsample coherent semantic regions while preserving boundaries.

paragraphs: SCONE addresses the next-best-view problem: choosing where a depth sensor should move to improve a three-dimensional reconstruction. Volumetric scene representations support path planning, while surface representations can provide better accuracy but scale poorly and restrict sensor poses. The paper connects these representations by estimating surface coverage through volumetric integration.

The approach uses two neural modules. One predicts occupancy probabilities throughout the scene volume. For a proposed camera pose, the other samples points according to those probabilities and uses self-attention to predict their visibility. Integrating these visibility estimates yields an estimated gain in surface coverage, and the method selects the pose with the greatest gain.

Monte Carlo integration makes the surface-oriented objective usable with a volumetric representation. SCONE accepts depth-sensor point clouds and camera poses, handles free camera motion, and is designed to scale to large scenes. The authors demonstrate it on a new dataset of large, complex three-dimensional scenes, supporting its use for view planning beyond tightly constrained camera configurations.
neurips-2022-scone-surface-coverage-opti.tldr: SCONE selects sensor viewpoints by estimating surface-coverage gains through learned occupancy, visibility, and volumetric integration.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning must balance improving each client’s own model with improving a shared model that helps other clients. These objectives can disagree when clients differ. This paper develops a method that lets clients automatically adjust that balance using uncertainty, drawing inspiration from Bayesian hierarchical models.

The method quantifies variation both between clients and within each client. Greater variation across clients indicates a greater need for personalization. These uncertainty estimates guide local training steps and the rule for combining client contributions. As a result, the balance between personal and global learning is built into training and aggregation rather than determined only through conventional fine-tuning and sample counts.

Experiments use synthetic data, Amazon Alexa audio, and public datasets including MNIST, FEMNIST, CIFAR10, and Sent140. The authors report that the method can significantly improve personalization performance over existing counterparts. The findings support uncertainty as a useful signal for deciding how much clients should share and how much their models should adapt to their own data.
neurips-2022-self-aware-personalized-fed.tldr: Client-level uncertainty guides the balance between personalized and shared federated learning, improving personalization in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Structured prediction involves outputs whose parts depend on one another. Energy networks can express these dependencies, but using gradient-based inference to obtain predictions can be slow and unstable. This paper proposes Structured Energy As Loss, or SEAL, to retain the usefulness of energy modeling while changing how predictions are produced.

SEAL uses an energy network as a trainable loss for a separate task network. The task network learns under this loss and then produces predictions through a forward pass. The framework supports several ways to train the loss network, including margin-based, regression, and noise-contrastive strategies, giving model designers multiple choices within the same approach.

Evaluations cover multi-label classification, semantic role labeling, and image segmentation. The authors report faster inference than gradient-based inference and significant performance gains over the evaluated baselines. The central contribution is a division of labor: a flexible learned energy function shapes training, while a separate prediction network supplies the outputs efficiently at inference time.
neurips-2022-structured-energy-network-a.tldr: SEAL trains a prediction network with a learned energy-based loss, enabling faster forward-pass inference and reported performance gains.

paragraphs: Learning physical dynamics from observed trajectories becomes difficult when measurements are noisy and sparse. This paper develops a probabilistic model for conservative and dissipative systems using Hamiltonian structure. The aim is to learn motion while incorporating the geometry associated with the system’s energy-based description.

The authors introduce a Gaussian process prior with symplectic structure for Hamiltonian systems that can include additive dissipation. They then derive a spectral representation, called Symplectic Spectrum Gaussian Processes, using random Fourier features that preserve this structure. This construction supports an efficient variational inference procedure in which ordinary differential equation solvers simulate the dynamics during training.

Experiments on several physical systems show strong prediction performance from noisy, sparse observations, with predicted dynamics following energy conservation or dissipation laws. The approach matters because its physical structure is part of the probabilistic model used for learning. The stated treatment of dissipative behavior specifically uses additive dissipation, defining the setting in which the Hamiltonian prior is extended.
neurips-2022-symplectic-spectrum-gaussia.tldr: Symplectic Gaussian processes learn energy-structured dynamics from sparse, noisy trajectories, including systems with additive dissipation.

paragraphs: Meta-learning uses experience across tasks to support adaptation to new tasks with little data. Sharing information during training can expose sensitive properties of an entire task dataset. This paper targets task-level differential privacy, extending protection beyond individual records to the dataset associated with each task.

For learning a single meta model, the authors provide privacy and utility guarantees assuming convex, Lipschitz losses. These assumptions avoid the smoothness and quadratic-growth requirements used in earlier utility guarantees. The distinction in privacy scope also matters: protecting records individually does not necessarily protect aggregate information about the task as a whole.

The paper additionally proposes a private clustering-based algorithm for learning multiple meta models. This can provide substantial accuracy gains when a single model does not represent the task distribution well. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms. Together, the contributions address both the unit of privacy protection and the possibility that different groups of tasks need different shared models.
neurips-2022-task-level-differentially-p.tldr: Task-level private meta-learning protects whole task datasets and supports either one shared model or multiple privately clustered models.

paragraphs: WebShop is a simulated shopping environment for evaluating agents that turn language instructions into sequences of web actions. It contains 1.18 million real products and 12,087 crowdsourced instructions. Agents must navigate different page types, search, customize products, and complete purchases that satisfy the requested requirements.

The tasks combine language understanding with decision making. An agent may need to interpret several constraints together, revise a search query, handle noisy webpage text, and explore strategically. The authors collect more than 1,600 human trajectories to validate the benchmark and train and evaluate agents using reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and pretrained image and language models.

The strongest reported model succeeds on 29% of tasks, outperforming rule heuristics but remaining below expert humans at 59%. Analyses of trajectories and model components help explain this gap. An agent trained in WebShop also shows non-trivial transfer to Amazon and eBay, suggesting potential practical value while leaving a substantial benchmark gap to human performance.
neurips-2022-webshop-towards-scalable-re.tldr: WebShop benchmarks instruction-following shopping agents at scale, revealing a large human-performance gap and some transfer to real websites.
